Supreme Court of Florida  
 
____________ 
 
No. SC2024 -0025 
____________ 
 
UNIVERSAL PROPERTY & CASUALTY INSURANCE COMPANY , 
Petitioner,  
 
vs. 
 
REBECCA HUGHES,  
Respondent.  
 
October 22, 2026  
 
COURIEL, C.J. 
 This is an i nsurance dispute .  A statute requir es that a 
claimant notify  an insurer , by way of a state regulator,  before filing 
a lawsuit .  We must decide whether that  statutory presuit notice 
requirement applies retroactively ; that is, whether it applies to an 
action for breach of an insurance policy that was issued before the 
statute w ent into effect.1  We find that the statute  does not  apply , 
and in doing so approve the decision of the Sixth District Court of 
 
 1.  We have jurisdiction.  Art. V, § 3(b)(4), Fla. Const.  
- 2 - Appeal .  See Hughes v. Universal Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. , 374 So. 3d 
900, 910 (Fla. 6th D CA 2023).  
I 
From April 24, 2019,  to April 24, 2020, Rebecca Hughes had a 
homeowners insurance policy with Universal  Property & Casualty 
Insurance Company .  On May 29, 2019, she  filed a claim for water 
damage.  Universal reviewed the claim and issued payment .  
Hughes objected  to the amount as insufficient.  R elying on three 
bids she obtained for the work, Hughes demanded more .   
On July 1, 2021, section 627.70152, Florida Statutes, went 
into effect.  Its enactment was part of a larger legislative effort to 
revise the statutes that govern property insurance policies, including the ones about who pays attorney s’ fees, notice periods 
for bringing claims, alternative dispute resolution, lawsuits involving property insurance policies, and when to consolidate  legal 
actions.   
Four of its  subsections matter here .   
Section 627.70152(1) , Florida Statutes (2021),  states that the 
provision  “applies exclusively to all suits not brought by an assignee 
- 3 - arising under a residential or commercial property insurance 
policy.”   
Section 627.70152(3)  creates the presuit notice requirement.  
It says:  
(3) NOTICE .— 
(a) As a condition  precedent to filing a suit under a 
property insurance policy, a claimant must provide the 
department[2] with written notice of intent to initiate 
litigation on a form provided by the department.  Such 
notice must be given at least 10 business days before filing suit under the policy, but may not be given before the insurer has made a determination of coverage under s. 627.70131.  
 Id.  Subsection (3)(a) further sets forth the specific information that 
must be included in the notice.  And subsection (3)(b) tolls the 
statute of limitations, in certain circumstances, for claims subject 
to the presuit notice requirement.    Section 627.70152(5) says what happens when a  claim ant 
sues without first providing the required notice:   
(5) DISMISSAL OF SUIT .—A court must dismiss without 
prejudice any claimant ’s suit relating to a claim for which 
a notice of intent to initiate litigation was not given as 
required by this section or if such suit is commenced 
 
 2.  That is, the Department of Financial Services, which must 
then notify the insurer.  § 627.70152(3).    
- 4 - before the expiration of any time period provided under 
subsection (4), as applicable.  
  Section 627.70152(8) , Florida Statutes (2021) (repealed 2022),  
contain ed multiple provisions concerning a claimant’s ability to 
recover attorneys’ fees.  Of note was  section 627.70152(8)(b), which 
provide d that where a claimant’s lawsuit was  dismissed for failure 
to provide notice, the claimant could not recover any attorneys’ fees 
incurred for services rendered before the dismissal.
3   
The Sixth District summarized :  
Before section 627.70152’s enactment, an insurer had a single opportunity to evaluate and pay an insurance claim before being sued —when the insured made the 
claim.   If an insurer wrongfully denied a claim, the 
 
 3.  There is also s ection 627.70152(4), which imposes a duty 
on insurers to create procedures to investigate and evaluate claims asserted in presuit notices and to respond in writing to such notices.    
If the insurer previously denied coverage for the claim, it must 
respond by either accepting coverage, continuing to deny coverage, or asserting the right to reinspect the damaged property.  § 627.70152(4)(a)1. –3.  
If the insurer did not completely deny coverage of an initial 
claim, it must respond to a presuit notice with a settlement offer or 
by demanding that the claimant participate in an alternative 
dispute resolution process.  § 627.70152(4)(b).  
The appraisal process will toll the statute of limitations for up 
to the conclusion of the 90- day period after the notice of intent, 
after which time the insured may immediately file suit without 
further notice.  Id.   
- 5 - insured immediately possessed a cause of action against 
the insurance company for breach of the insurance policy, and the insured could immediately sue the insurance company to recover damages and attorneys’ fees.  After section 627.70152 ’s enactment, an insurer 
now has a second opportunity to evaluate and pay a claim and to prevent the insured from asserting a cause 
of action for breach of the insurance policy.  Specifically, 
after the insurer receives a pre -suit notice of intent to 
litigate, the insurer has an additional 10 business days 
to accept coverage and pay the claim.   If the insurer pays 
the claim during that period, the insured ’s cause of 
action will never ripen and the claim for attorneys’ fees the insured otherwise would have possessed will never exist.  
 Hughes , 374 So. 3d at 904.     
 On August 4, 2021, Hughes filed a  lawsuit against Universal  
about the claim she had filed in 2019 .  She did not file a section 
627.70152 notice prior to suit.   Universal moved to dismiss on that 
basis.  Hughes contended that section 627.70152 did not apply 
retroactively to policies, like hers,  purchased before the statute 
went into effect.  The trial court disagreed and dismissed her  
complaint  without prejudice.  
Hughes appealed .  While that was pending , the Fourth District 
Court of Appeal  decided Cole v. Universal Property & Casualty 
Insurance Co. , 363 So. 3d 1089 (Fla. 4th D CA 2023).   In Cole, the 
Fourth District found the presuit notice requirement applied 
- 6 - retroactively to existing policies in effect at the time of enactment 
and upheld the trial court’s dismissal (without prejudice) of a suit 
based upon the plaintiff’s failure to file section 627.70152 presuit notice.  Id. at 1095.  The Fourth District found that the Legislature , 
in subsections (1) and  (3), expressed a clear intent to have the 
statute apply retroactively .  Specifically, the court found evidence of 
the Legislature’s intent to focus on suits as the object of the law in 
subsection (1)’s statement that the statute “applies exclusively to all suits . . . arising under a residential or commercial property 
insurance policy.”  Id. at 1093 (quoting § 627.70152(1) ).  The court 
also found evidence of intent in the text of subsection (3) , which 
says, “[a]s a condition precedent to filing a suit under a property 
insurance policy, a claimant must provide the department with written notice of intent to initiate litigation on a form provided by the department.”   Id. at 1092 (quoting § 627.70152(3)(a)) .  From 
this, the court reasoned  that the notice requirement  “also applies to 
all policies, including those already in existence at the time of the statute’s effective date. ”  Id. at 1093 .  The court surmised that “[i] f 
the legislature had intended to limit this presuit notice provision to policies issued after the statute’s effective date, the legislature 
- 7 - would have included language stating so.”  Id.  
The Sixth District disagreed with Cole and sided with Hughes, 
reversing the trial court .  Hughes , 374 So. 3d at 910.  The Sixth 
District found no clear evidence of  the legislative intent for the 
statute  to apply retroactively .  Id. at 906.  Instead, the court 
determined that the “all suits” language in section 627.70152(1) 
merely referred to the types of cases and policies to which the 
statute applies—cases involving residential or commercial 
insurance policies not brought by assignees.  Id. at 906 -07.  
Further, the Sixth District rejected the Fourth District’s  analysis of 
section 627.70152(3)(a) , finding that it “ invert [ed] Florida Supreme 
Court precedent requiring clear evidence of intent for a statute to apply retroactively, not a lack of evidence that the statute applies only prospectively. ”  Id. at 907.   The court explained that “[t] he 
absence of language in a statute stating that the statute is inapplicable to existing insurance policies does not constitute clear evidence of retroactive intent.”   Id. (citing Fla. Ins. Guar . Ass’n v. 
Devon Neighborhood Ass’n , 67 So. 3d 187, 197  (Fla. 2011)).  
After Cole and Hughes , the First, Second, Third, and Fifth 
District Courts  of Appeal  also weighed in on section 627.70152’s 
- 8 - retroactivity.  In Cantens v. Certain Underwriters at Lloyd’s London , 
388 So. 3d 242 (Fla. 3d D CA 2024), the Third District agreed with 
the Fourth District that section 627.70152 had retroactive 
application, largely adopting the reasoning of the Fourth District.  
Conversely, the First, Second , and Fifth Districts held that section 
627.70152 did not apply retroactively, agreeing with the analysis of 
the Sixth District.  See Priest v. State Farm Fla. Ins. Co. , No. 
1D2024 -1577, 2026 WL 1408204 (Fla. 1st DCA May 20, 2026); Buis 
v. Universal Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. , 394 So. 3d 738 (Fla. 2d D CA 
2024); Smith v. Universal Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co., 396 So. 3d 860 (Fla. 
5th DCA 2024).  
II 
A 
As a general rule, “the statute in effect at the time an 
insurance contract is executed governs substantive issues arising in 
connection with that contract.”  Hassen v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 674 So. 2d 106, 108 (Fla. 1996).
4  The parties agree that 
 
 4.  The conflict issue presents a pure question of law that is 
subject to de novo review.  See L. Offs. of Herssein & Herssein, P.A. 
v. United Servs. Auto. Ass’n , 271 So. 3d 889, 893 (Fla. 2018).   
- 9 - the operat ive date for analyzing the statute at issue is April 24, 
2019 , the date on which the policy was issued .  Section 627.70152 
went into effect on  July 1, 2021.  So  Universal  admits  that it seeks 
to apply section 627.70152 retroactively to Hughes’s suit  for breach 
of her 2019 policy .   
We have applied  a two -step test when deciding  whether a 
statute has retroactive application: “First, the Court must ascertain 
whether the Legislature intended for the statute to apply retroactively.  Second, if such an intent is clearly expressed, the Court must determine whether retroactive applicat ion would violate 
any constitutional principles.”  Menendez v. Progressive Exp. Ins.  
Co., 35 So. 3d 873, 877 (Fla. 2010)  (citing Metro . Dade County v. 
Chase Fed . Hous . Corp., 737 So. 2d 494, 499 (Fla. 1999)) .
5  As our 
traditional description of that second step suggests, at the first  
 
 5.  In Menendez , we held that section 627.736(11), Florida 
Statutes (2001) , which required written notice to an auto insurer 
before filing a suit against the insurer, did not apply retroactively to 
insurance policies issued before that statute took effect.  35 So. 3d 
at 875.  In so holding, we set forth the two -part test invoked above.  
Id. at 877; accord Chase Fed. , 737 So. 2d at  499; see also Smiley v. 
State , 966 So. 2d 330, 336 (Fla. 2007); Old Port Cove Holdings, Inc. 
v. Old Port Cove Condo. Ass’n One, 986 So. 2d 1279, 1284 (Fla. 2008).  
- 10 - step, there is no substitute for a clear legislative command in 
determining whether the Legislature provided for retroactive 
application.    
It also bears emphasizing that , in looking for “intent” in the 
“plain language of the statute,” see  Devon , 67 So. 3d at 194,  we do 
so using “the supremacy -of-the-text principle, recognizing that ‘ [t]he 
words of a governing text are of paramount concern, and what they convey, in their context, is what the text means ,’ ” Coates v. R.J. 
Reynolds Tobacco Co. , 365 So. 3d 353, 354 (Fla. 2023) (alteration in 
original) (quoting Levy v. Levy, 326 So. 3d 678, 681 (Fla. 2021)).   
The goal , as always,  is to “look for the original meaning of the 
statutory text to keep us from overriding the bargain struck in the Legislature and signed by the Governor, that is, the law that governs us.”  Tomlinson v. State, 369 So. 3d 1142, 1146 (Fla. 2023)  
(citing New Prime Inc. v. Oliveira , 586 U.S. 105, 113 (2019)) .  
Further, we have cautioned against the error of finding intent beyond the words of the statutory text.  See, e.g. , Gov’t Emps.  Ins. 
Co. v. Glassco Inc. , 394 So. 3d 1115, 1120 (Fla. 2024) (“A court can 
look to statutory purpose to illuminate the meaning of the statutory text, but statutory purpose cannot be invoked to justify ignoring the 
- 11 - text—the Legislature’s actual work product.”).  Thus, what we 
properly  consider  under the first prong is whether the Legislature 
has manifested  a clear command for retroactivity in the statutory 
text.   
Here, as to subsection (1) , that is not the case.   It says that the 
section “applies exclusively to all suits not brought by an assignee 
arising under a residential or commercial property insurance policy.”  § 627.70152(1).  This  addresses the types of cases and 
policies to which the statute applies: cases involving residential or 
commercial insurance policies not brought by assignees.  The fact that the L egislature used the phrase  “all suits” in this context does 
not transform this subsection into a clear command to apply section 627.70152 retroactively.  We agree with the Second District that “[t]here is nothing in the language of the statute to indicate that the phrase ‘ all suits ’ is serving another purpose of expanding 
its reach to those suits based on policies that both predate and postdate the enactment of the statute.”  Buis, 394 So. 3d at 741.   
Neither does s ubsection (3) , the notice requirement itself,  
provide a clear command  about retroactivity .  That subsection 
requires that, at least ten days before filing suit , notice must be 
- 12 - provided to the Department of Financial Services.  
§ 627.70152(3)(a).  The subsection then sets forth in detail what 
information must be included in the notice.  Id.  And subsection 
(3)(b) tolls the statute of limitations, in certain circumstances.   
As noted above, in Cole,  the Fourth  District focused  on part of 
this subsection that says,  “[a]s a condition precedent to filing a suit 
under a property insurance policy, a claimant must provide the 
department with written notice of intent to initiate litigation on a 
form provided by the department.”  § 627.70152(3)(a).  Based on this, the Cole court found that section 627.70152 “also applies to all 
policies, including those already in existence at the time of the statute ’s effective date.”  363 So. 3d at 1093.  The court reasoned  
that, “[i]f the legislature had intended to limit this presuit  notice 
provision to policies issued after the statute’s effective date, the legislature would have included language stating so.”  Id.   
Like the Sixth District, we reject this analysis, which turns our 
precedent on its head.  At the first step of Menendez , we look for 
“clear evidence of legislative intent to apply the statute retrospectively .”  Devon , 67 So. 3d at 194 (quoting Chase Fed ., 737 
So. 2d at 499) .  And “the absence of a statement in the act .  . . does 
- 13 - not constitute clear evidence of retroactive intent.”  Id.  at 197  
(emphasis omitted) .  “In short, clear evidence must consist of more 
than silence.”  Hughes , 374 So. 3d at 907.   
Finally, the statute has an effective date, which this Court has 
long considered to be evidence against retroactive application.  See 
Devon , 67 So. 3d at 196 (“We have noted that the Legislature’s 
inclusion of an effective date for an amendment is considered to be evidence rebutting intent for retroactive application of a law.”  (citing 
State Dep’t of Rev. v. Zuckerman -Vernon  Corp. , 354 So. 2d 353, 358 
(Fla. 1977) ). 
So, on its face, no provision of s ection 627.70152 speaks to  
application of the statute to insurance policies issued before the statute’s effective date.   And n othing in our precedent demands that 
we disturb that silence.  The correct answer is to respect the 
Legislature’s choice not to clearly require retroactive application of 
the statute. 
B 
We briefly consider Universal ’s argument that our Menendez 
test does not apply here because section 627.70152’s presuit notice 
requirement is procedural, not substantive.     
- 14 - If the presuit notice requirement stood by itself, Universal 
might have a point.  But when we decide  whether a statu te is 
substantive in deter mining whether it should be given retroactive 
effect, we look at it  “as a whole.”  Menendez , 35 So. 3d at 8 79-80.  
And as the Sixth District explained, viewed as a whole, section 
627.70152 “transformed an insured’s ability to sue an insurance 
company under a property insurance policy and an insurer’s 
obligations to respond to and pay insurance claims.”  Hughes , 374 
So. 3d at 904.   The statute (1)  imposes a penalty of dismissal 
without prejudice for failing to comply with the presuit notice requirement ; (2) (under the now repealed subsection (8)(b)) provided 
that when a claimant’s lawsuit was dismissed for failure to provide 
notice, the claimant could not recover any attorneys’ fees incurred for services rendered before the dismissal; (3)  provides a safe harbor 
for insurers and grants them additional time to pay benefits; and (4) delays an insured’s right to initiate a lawsuit.  See supra pp.  2-5.  
Given these legal effects, we find no reason to disturb the Sixth District’s conclusion  that section 627.70152 “significantly alters an 
insurer’s obligation to pay and an insured ’s right to sue under a 
property insurance policy.”  Hughes , 374 So. 3d at 904.   
- 15 - III 
We approve the decision of the Sixth District in Hughes  to the 
extent it is consistent with this decision.   We disapprove the 
decision of the Fourth District in Cole.   
It is so ordered.  
LABARGA, MUÑIZ, GROSSHANS, FRANCIS, and BARRIOS, JJ., 
concur.  
TANENBAUM, J., concurs with an opinion.  
 
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE REHEARING MOTION AND, IF FILED, DETERMINED.  
 TANENBAUM, J., concurring.  
 
Menendez  is not needed to answer the question here.  The 
Legislature has told us expressly that “[e]ach amendment” to the 
insurance code —including the addition of section 627.70152, 
Florida Statutes —“shall be construed to operate prospectively, 
unless a contrary l egislative intent is specified .”  § 624.21, Fla. Stat. 
(emphasis supplied); cf.  Hassen v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. , 
674 So. 2d 106, 108 (Fla. 1996) (“It is a well established rule of statutory construction that, in the absence of an express legislative 
statement to the contrary, an enactment that affects substantive rights or creates new obligations or liabilities is presumed to apply 
- 16 - prospectively.” (emphasis supplied)).  
The Legislature heavily regulates the insurance industry 
(including its issuance of insurance policies and the handling of 
claims), and the industry adopts standard policy language and claims -handling processes against the regulatory backdrop extant 
at a g iven time.  For this reason, “it is generally accepted that the 
statute in effect at the time an insurance contract is executed governs substantive issues arising in connection with that contract.”  Hassen , 674 So. 2d at 108.  The Legislature undoubtedly 
is aware of this approach, an awareness likely reflected in section 624.21, Florida Statutes, originally enacted in 1982.  
In the light of this, we are not going to find the retroactivity 
specification mandated by section 624.21 in the Legislature’s silence or merely by inference.  There is no express legislative 
command to apply the new section 627.70152 retrospectively —e.g. , 
a statement that it applies to all policies active (or open claims, or  
accrued causes of action) when the law goes into effect —so the 
provision applies only prospectively, to policies issued after the 
provision’s effective date, as the Legislature has directed.  
As to the assertion that section 627.70152 is procedural, the 
- 17 - provision is not meaningfully different from the pre -suit notice 
requirement set out in section 768.57, Florida Statutes (1985).  And 
we held that the former statute was substantive, not procedural.  See Williams v. Campagnulo, 588 So. 2d 982, 983 (Fla. 1991) (“The statute was intended to address a legitimate legislative policy decision relating to medical malpractice and established a process 
intended to promote the settlement of meritorious claims at an early 
stage without th e necessity of a full adversarial proceeding.”).  
In turn, I agree with the Sixth District’s conclusion that the 
statute does not apply to Hughes’s suit.

for Amicus Curiae American Adjuster Association

items.summary:
The Florida Supreme Court held that section 627.70152’s presuit notice requirement does not apply retroactively to a property-insurance policy issued before the statute took effect on July 1, 2021. The statutory text contains no clear command for retroactivity. Viewed as a whole, the statute substantively alters the insured’s right to sue and the insurer’s obligations, rather than merely prescribing procedure. The court approved Hughes to the extent consistent with its decision and disapproved Cole. Justice Tanenbaum separately concurred, relying on the Insurance Code’s express prospectivity provision.

Holding: The section 627.70152 presuit notice requirement does not apply to the claim under the policy issued before the statute’s July 1, 2021 effective date.

Disposition: Sixth DCA decision approved to the extent consistent; Fourth DCA decision in Cole disapproved.

IN RE: AMENDMENTS TO  RULES REGULATING THE FLORIDA 
BAR – RULE 20 -6.1. 
 
October 22, 2026  
 
PER CURIAM.  
The Florida Bar filed a petition  proposing amendments to Rule 
Regulating The Florida Bar 20 -6.1 (Continuing Education; 
Generally ).1  Consistent with r ule 1 -12.1(g), the Bar published 
formal notice of its intent to file the proposed amendments  on its 
website and in The Florida Bar News.  The notice directed interested 
parties to file comments directly with the Court.  No comments were received.  Having considered the proposal, we adopt the 
amendments to  rule 20 -6.1 as proposed .   
Specifically, we amend rule 20 -6.1 to create a new subdivision 
(a) (Lecture Credit) to  allow Florida Registered Paralegals to receive 
 
 1.  We have jurisdiction.  See art. V, § 15, Fla. Const.; see also 
R. Regulating Fla. Bar 1 -12.1.  
- 2 - lecture credit for approved seminars for up to 3 credit hours for 
each 50 minutes of lecture at basic seminars or up to 5 credit hours for each 50 minutes of lecture time at intermediate seminars.   
We also adopt a new subdivision (b) (Extensions) that allow s 
the Executive Director or Board of Governors to permit extensions 
of the time for completion for continuing education requirements in 
certain circumstances.   
Last, we add language to clarify that “[i]f a Florida Registered 
Paralegal completes more than 30 credit hours during any reporting 
cycle, the excess credits cannot be carried over to the next reporting cycle.”  
Accordingly, the Rules Regulating The Florida Bar  are 
amended as set forth in  the appendix to this opinion.  New language 
is indicated  by underscoring; deletions are indicated  by struck -
through type.  The amendments become effective December  21, 
2026 , at 12:01 a.m . 
It is so ordered.  
COURIEL, C.J., and LABARGA, MUÑIZ, GROSSHANS, FRANCIS, 
and BARRIOS, JJ., concur.  
TANENBAUM, J., dissents with an opinion.  
 
- 3 - THE FILING OF A MOTION FOR REHEARING SHALL NOT ALTER 
THE EFFECTIVE DATE OF THESE AMENDMENTS.  
 TANENBAUM, J., dissenting.  
 
Chapter 20 should be removed from the Rules Regulating the 
Florida Bar.  Paralegals, by definition, are not lawyers— so are not 
admitted to practice law.  That means they are beyond this court’s 
regulatory authority.  See Art. V, §  15, Fla. Const. (“The supreme 
court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to regulate the admission of 
persons to the practice of law and the discipline of  persons 
admitted .” (emphasis supplied)); see also Fla. Bar v. Hidalgo , 435 
So. 3d 627, 628 (Fla. 2026) (Tanenbaum, J., dissenting) (challenging this court’s authority to regulate non -lawyers at all).  
The bar, an administrative arm of this court charged with implementing the just -highlighted text, should remain focused on 
accomplishing its core mission.  At the same time, it should avoid 
developing and running a money- raising operation beyond that 
mission, which is what the Florida Registered Paralegal Program appears to be.  
Original Proceeding –  Florida Rules Regulating The  Florida Bar  
Michael Fox Orr, President, Paige Greenlee, President -elect, Joshua 
E. Doyle, Executive Director, Elizabeth Clark Tarbert, Division 
- 4 - Director, Lawyer Regulation, and Kelly N. Smith, Senior Attorney, 
The Florida Bar, Tallahassee, Florida,  
 
for Petitione r 
 
- 5 - APPENDIX  
 
RULE 20- 6.1. GENERALLY  
Florida Registered Paralegals must complete a minimum of 30 
hours of continuing education every 3 years, 5 hours of which must 
be in legal ethics or professionalism and 3 hours of which must be 
in technology.  Acceptable courses include those approved for credit 
by The Florida Bar, the National Association of Legal Assistants 
(NALA), or the National Federation of Paralegal Associations (NFPA).  
If a Florida Registered Paralegal completes more than 30 credit 
hours during any reporting cycle, the excess credits cannot be 
carried over to the next reporting cycle.   A Florida Registered 
Paralegal who resigns or whose status has been revoked but is 
otherwise eligible for re- registration must complete at least 10 
hours of continuing education for each year the Florida Registered Paralegal was previously registered in or der to  be eligible for re -
registration.  The new registration will be revoked unless the continuing education hours are completed before the re- registration 
application and posted on The Florida Bar website within 30 days of the effective date of the re- registration.  The Florida Registered 
Paralegal will be given a new 3 -year continuing education cycle on 
re-registration.  
(a) Lecture Credit.  A Florida Registered Paralegal may 
receive continuing education credit after satisfactory performance 
as a lecturer in an approved course.  Credit will be approved for up 
to 3 credit hours for each 50 minutes of lecture time at basic 
seminars, or up to 5 credit hours for each 50 minutes of lecture 
time at intermediate seminars.    
(b) Extensions.   The Florida Bar Executive Director or Board 
of Governors may adjust the time for completion for continuing 
education requirements for good cause shown, which may include, 
but is not limited to:  
(1)  national or regional emergency;  
(2)  flood, fire, hurricane, extended extreme weather, or 
explosion;  
(3)  disease, epidemic, pandemic, or quarantine;  
- 6 - (4)  war, invasion, or terrorist threats or acts;  
(5)  extended riots, protest, civil unrest, civil strife, or 
political unrest; or 
(6)  local, state, federal, or foreign government 
recommendation, regulation, mandate, order, law, statute, or 
advisory.  
Requests for extensions from individual members will not be 
considered.  
 
Comment  
[No Change]

items.summary:
Effective December 21, 2026, at 12:01 a.m., amended rule 20-6.1 permits lecture credit for Florida Registered Paralegals, authorizes continuing-education completion extensions for good cause through the Bar’s Executive Director or Board of Governors, and clarifies that excess credits cannot carry forward. The amendment excludes individual extension requests. Justice Tanenbaum dissented, questioning the court’s authority to regulate paralegals.

Holding: Rule 20-6.1 amended to address lecture credit, extensions, and noncarryover of excess credits.

Disposition: Amendments adopted, effective December 21, 2026, at 12:01 a.m.

FIRST DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
No. 1D20 25-3177 
_____________________________  
 
CLINICAL SPECIALTY INFUSIONS 
OF DALLAS , LLC,  
 
Appellant,  
 
v. 
 
FLORIDA OFFICE OF INSURANCE 
REGULATION , 
 
Appellee.  
_____________________________  
 
 On appeal from the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation.  
Michael Yaworsky, Commissioner.  
 
October 21, 2026  
  P
ER CURIAM .  
 
Appellant Clinical Specialty Infusions of Dallas, LLC (CSI) 
appeals the denial of its petition for declaratory statement by the 
Florida Office of Insurance Regulation (OIR).  CSI argues that it 
was entitled to a declaratory statement under section 120.565, 
Florida Statutes (20 25).  We find that OIR’s interpretation of 
sections 120.565 and 626.8825(2), Florida Statutes, and rule 28 -
105.001, Florida Administrative Code , was correct.  Thus, we 
affirm the administrative order denying the petition for 
declaratory statement.  See § 120.68(7)(d), Fla. Stat. (discussing 
when a district court may set aside agency action).  
2 We are required to affirm final agency action unless we find a 
ground for setting aside, modifying, remanding, or ordering agency 
action under a specified provision of section 120.68(7), Florida 
Statutes.  § 120.68(8), Fla. Stat.  Additionally, we are required to 
remand a case to the agency for further proceedings if the agency “erroneously interpreted a provision of law and a correct 
interpretation compels a particular action.”  § 120.68(7), Fla. Stat.   
In its petition, CSI sought OIR’s opinion on whether section 
626.8825(2)(g), Florida Statutes, mandated that an unnamed 
pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) must include CSI in its 
pharmacy benefit plan or program specialty network.  See  
§ 626.8825(1) (t)–(u) (defini ng pharmacy benefit manager and 
pharmacy benefit plan).  And CSI asked OIR to declare “that a 
PBM cannot legally exclude Petitioner, which complies with all 
applicable FDA standards and requirements, from a pharmacy 
benefits program plan or program specialty network.”  
OIR denied CSI’s petition in its order entered in November 
2025.  It found that CSI’s petition sought “a declaratory statement 
concerning the conduct of another person” and, as such, was 
invalid under rule 28 -105.001, Florida Administrative Code.
*  OIR 
reasoned that the statute at issue in CSI’s petition, section 
626.8825(2) (g), addressed “those terms that must be included in all 
contractual arrangements between a PBM and a pharmacy 
benefits plan or program.”  OIR found that CSI is a specialty 
pharmacy, as defined by section 465.003(20 )(a)4., Florida Statutes, 
but it “does not, however, purport to be a PBM or pharmacy benefits plan or program.”  Because section 626.8825(2)(g) “relates 
 
* Rule 28 -105.001 states:  
 
A declaratory statement is a means for resolving a 
controversy or answering questions or doubts concerning the applicability of statutory provisions, rules, or orders 
over which the agency has authority.  A petition for 
declaratory statement may be used to resolve questions or doubts as to how the statutes, rules, or orders may 
apply to the petitioner’s particular circumstances.  A 
declaratory statement is not the appropriate means for 
determining the conduct of another person. 
3 solely to the conduct of a PBM or pharmacy benefits plan or 
program, not the conduct of a pharmacy,” OIR found that CSI’s 
petition fell “outside the limited scope of a declaratory statement 
because Petitioner’s question regards the conduct of a third- party 
PBM, not the conduct of Petitioner.”   
A petition for declaratory statement may properly seek an 
opinion on the application of a statute to the petitioner’s particular 
circumstances that will be “of interest to others in the very limited group.”  ExxonMobil Oil Corp. v. State, Dep’t of Agric. & Consumer 
Servs. , 50 So. 3d 755, 758 (Fla. 1st DCA 2010) (quoting Florida  
Dep’t of Bus. & Pro. Regul., Div. of Pari-Mutuel Wagering v. Inv. 
Corp. of Palm Beach, 747 So. 2d 374, 385 (Fla. 1999)).  But w e 
agree with OIR’s application of section 120.565 to require that a 
petition for declaratory statement must apply to the petitioner’s 
particular circumstances so that the petitioner “may select a 
proper course of action,” and the petition may not seek an agency’s 
opinion solely to determine the application of a statute to a person 
other than the petitioner.  See Bd. of Cnty. Comm’rs Indian River 
Cnty. v. Graham, 191 So. 3d 890, 894 (Fla. 2016); Carr v. Old Port 
Cove Prop. Owners Ass’n, Inc., 8 So. 3d 403 , 404  (Fla. 4th DCA 
2009) ; see also  Nat’l Ass'n of Optometrists & Opticians v. Fla.  Dep’t 
of Health, Fla. Bd. of Optometry, 922 So. 2d 1060, 1062 (Fla. 1st 
DCA 2006)  (“A party who obtains a statement of an agency’s 
position in a declaratory statement may avoid costly administrative litigation by selecting the proper course of action in 
advance. ”).   
OIR correctly interpreted section 626.8825(2)(g) as not 
applicable to CSI’s particular circumstances — CSI’s asserted 
wrongful exclusion from a specialty pharmacy network.  The 
subsection only applies to contracts between PBMs and pharmacy 
benefit plans or programs.  Pharmacies like CSI are not regulated 
by the subsection.  Thus, CSI’s petition seeks an opinion solely 
about the actions of a PBM under a contract governed by the 
subsection to include or exclude a pharmacy.  CSI is not seeking 
an opinion to select its own proper course of action, but rather 
seeks an opinion about a PBM’s course of action.    
Because Appellant fails to establish that OIR erroneously 
interpreted section 120.565 to deny the petition on grounds that 
4 the petition exceeded the scope of a declaratory statement, the 
order on appeal is affirmed.    
AFFIRMED .   
BILBREY , TREADWELL , and NEFF, JJ.,  concur.  
 
_____________________________  
 
Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 
9.331.  
_____________________________  
 
 
William D. Hall, III of Jones Walker LLP, Tallahassee, for 
Appellant.  
 
Gregory J. Mill, Assistant General Counsel, and Genevieve 
McNalis, Assistant General Counsel, Florida Office of Insurance 
Regulation, Tallahassee, for Appellee.

items.summary:
The First DCA affirmed denial of a specialty pharmacy’s petition for an agency declaratory statement. Section 120.565 permits a petitioner to clarify how law applies to its own circumstances so it can choose a course of action; it does not permit a request solely about another person’s conduct. The contract provision at issue governed pharmacy benefit managers and benefit plans, rather than the pharmacy, so the request to determine a manager’s obligation to include the pharmacy exceeded the declaratory-statement procedure’s scope.

Holding: An agency declaratory statement may address the petitioner’s own circumstances, but not solely determine the statutory obligations of a third party.

Disposition: Affirmed denial of the petition for declaratory statement.

items.summary:
The Third DCA affirmed by citation to contractual deadline and notice principles. The cited authorities distinguish a deadline stated in business days from one stated in ordinary days, which generally run through midnight, and reject avoiding information and then denying notice. The opinion does not describe the Fyffes' contract or the underlying facts; the quoted payment terms belong to a cited decision.

Holding: Affirmance by citation to principles that contractual use of business days for one event but days for another may require different calculations, with ordinary calendar days extending to midnight, and that a person cannot avoid information and then deny notice. The decision supplies these authorities without a case-specific factual explanation.

items.summary:
In related probate appeals, the Third DCA affirmed because the appellant left an independent dispositive ground unchallenged. It dismissed review of unauthorized postjudgment relief and reconsideration orders, holding rule 1.540 unavailable in this nonadversary proceeding under the cited Probate Rules. Fee entitlement without a fixed amount was not yet appealable. The court did not independently decide the paternity issue on its merits; the unchallenged homestead determination controlled. The companion appeal from the postjudgment orders was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Holding: An appellant who attacks only one of multiple independent grounds supporting a judgment cannot obtain reversal while leaving another dispositive ground unchallenged. In this nonadversary probate proceeding, the court held rule1.540 unavailable under the Probate Rules and dismissed review of unauthorized postjudgment relief and reconsideration orders; rule9.170 did not supply jurisdiction over these nonfinal orders. Attorney-fee entitlement without a fixed amount was likewise not ripe for review. The paternity challenge could not disturb the unchallenged homestead determination.

Disposition: Affirmed in part, dismissed in part; postjudgment-order appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, judgment affirmed on unchallenged independent homestead ground, remaining individual-capacity/fee challenges disposed of as explained in the opinion.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 21, 2026 .

________________  
 
No. 3D25 -1826  
Lower Tribunal No. 21-16120 -CA-01 
________________  
 
 
Citizens Property Insurance Corporation , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Rosanna Weber, et al. , 
Appellee s. 
 
 
 
An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Reemberto 
Diaz, Judge.  
 
Traub Lieberman Straus & Shrewsberry LLP and C. Ryan Jones and 
David T. Burr (St. Petersburg) , for appellant.  
 
Alvarez, Feltman, Da Silva & Costa, PL and Paul B . Feltman , for 
appellee s. 
 
 
Before  GORDO, LOBREE and BOKOR , JJ. 
 
PER CURIAM.  
 2 Citizens Property Insurance Corporation appeals a final judgment 
awarding attorney’s fees and costs in favor of its insureds, appellees 
Rosanna and Randy Weber, challenging the award of a contingency fee 
multiplier to the Webers’ trial co -counsel, Alvarez Feltman Da Silva & Costa, 
PLLC, and the award of post -judgment interest calculated at a fixed rate.1  
Because the trial court’s application of a contingency fee multiplier is 
supported by competent, substantial evidence, we affirm the final judgment 
awarding attorney’s fees and costs.  However, t he Webers commendably 
acknowledge that the final judgment erroneously provides that post -
judgment interest is to be calculated at a constant rate until the judgment is 
satisfied .  See § 55.03(3), Fla. Stat. (2025) (“ The interest rate is established 
at the time a judgment is obtained and such interest rate shall be adjusted 
annually on January 1 of each year in accordance with the interest rate in 
effect on that date as set by the Chief Financial Officer until the judg ment is 
 
1 “‘Both the fee award and application of a multiplier are reviewed for an 
abuse of discretion,’ and therefore must be supported by competent, 
substantial evidence.” Little v. Bath & Kitchen Boutique, LLC , 435 So. 3d 
1142, 1144 n.1 (Fla. 3d DCA 2026) (citation omitted) (quoting Certain 
Underwriters at Lloyd's London v. Candelaria , 339 So. 3d 463, 467 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2022)) ; see also Universal Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. v. Medero , 406 So. 3d 
323, 326 (Fla. 3d DCA 2025) (“ Although a trial court’s determination to apply 
a multiplier to the lodestar amount is reviewed for an abuse of discretion, the 
trial court’s findings as to the multiplier itself must be supported by competent 
substantial evidence.”).  
 3 paid . . . .”);  Townsend v. R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. , 192 So. 3d 1223, 
1224 –25 (Fla. 2016) .  Accordingly, we remand  with directions to amend the 
final judgment to provide for a variable rate of interest in accordance with 
section 55.03(3).  
Affirmed in part,  reversed in part,  and remanded with directions.

items.summary:
The Third DCA affirmed the contingency fee multiplier because competent, substantial evidence supported it. It reversed the judgment's fixed postjudgment interest provision: section 55.03(3) (2025) requires adjustment each January 1 to the rate then set by the Chief Financial Officer until payment. The case was remanded to amend that provision; the decision does not establish a general entitlement to a multiplier.

Holding: The contingency fee multiplier was affirmed as supported by competent substantial evidence under abuse-of-discretion review. A judgment could not freeze postjudgment interest at its initial rate until payment: section 55.03(3) (2025) requires annual adjustment on January 1 using the rate then in effect as set by the Chief Financial Officer.

Disposition: Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded with directions to amend the judgment for variable postjudgment interest under section 55.03(3).

 2 Affirmed.   See § 624.155(3)(b)1 .,2.,4., Fla. Stat.  (2020)  (“The notice . . 
. shall state with specificity the following information  . . . 1. The statutory 
provision, including the specific language of the statute, which the authorized 
insurer allegedly violated.   2. The facts and circumstances giving rise to the 
violation.  . . . 4. Reference to specific policy language that is relevant to the 
violation, if any. ”); Julien v. United Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. , 311 So. 3d 875, 
879 (Fla. 4th DCA 2021) (affirming dismissal of insured’s statutory bad faith 
claim where civil remedy notice failed to specify statutory and policy 
provisions at issue ); Demase v. State Farm Fl a. Ins. Co. , 351 So. 3d 136 , 
138 (Fla. 5th DCA 2022)  (concluding that even under “more lenient 
substantial compliance test” insured’s bad faith claim failed because civil 
remedy notice did not comply with section 624.155’s specificity 
requirements); Bank of Am., N.A. v. Bank of N.Y. Mellon , 338 So. 3d 338, 
341 n.2 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022)  (“A trial court does not abuse its discretion in 
denying a motion for reconsideration or rehearing which raises an issue that 
could have [been], but wasn ’t, raised in the initial motion or at the initial 
hearing .”); Simeon, Inc. v. Cox , 671 So. 2d 158, 160 (Fla. 1996)  (holding that 
to comply with the  requirements  of section 768.72, Florida Statutes, “ a 
plaintiff must obtain leave from the trial court to amend the complaint before 
punitive damages may be asserted . . . . [A] ny punitive damages claim alleged 
 3 prior to a party asking for and receiving leave of the court must be dismissed 
or stricken .” (citations omitted) ; Roberts v. Int’l Speedway Corp. , 542 So. 2d 
446 (Fla. 5th DCA 1989)  (explaining that order denying motion to assess 
interest constituted final order where nothing else remained to be done in the 
cause).

items.summary:
The Third DCA affirmed with citations addressing specificity in statutory bad-faith civil remedy notices, reconsideration arguments that could have been raised earlier, leave to plead punitive damages, and finality of an order denying interest. Its quoted authorities require specific statutory and policy provisions in the notice and judicial leave before punitive damages are pleaded. The court supplied citation parentheticals rather than a factual narrative; the opinion does not explain which underlying facts implicated each ground.

Holding: Citation affirmance invoking notice specificity, reconsideration, punitive-damages pleading, and finality principles; no detailed factual application stated.

Disposition: Affirmed.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 21 , 2026.  
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________ 
 
No. 3D26 -0024  
Lower Tribunal No. 23-25057 -CA-01 
________________ 
 
 
Limousines of South Florida, Inc. , et al.,  
Appellant s, 
 
vs. 
 
Joseph Levit, et al. , 
Appellee s. 
 
 
 
 An Appeal from a non -final order from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Lourdes Simon , Judge.  
 
 Hamilton, Miller & Birthisel LLP,  and William  H. Edwards and Michael 
J. Dono , for appellant s. 
 
 Vladimir Tsirkin & Associates, P.A. , and Vladimir Tsirkin  (Hallandale 
Beach) , for appellee s. 
 Before  FERNANDEZ , GORDO and REBULL,  JJ.  
  GORDO, J.  
 
 2 ON MOTION FOR REHEARING AND CERTIFICATION OF QUESTIONS 
OF GREAT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE 
We deny the motion for rehearing and certification of questions of great 
public importance  but withdraw our previous opinion and substitute the 
following opinion in its stead.  
I. 
Limo usines  of South Florida  appeals a non-final order granting Levit’s  
request to amend the complaint to assert punitive damages .  We have 
jurisdiction. Fla. R. App. P. 9.130(a)(3)(G) .  Limousines argues that Levit 
failed to proffer sufficient evidence of intentional misconduct or  gross 
negligence  and establish  the requisite nexus between the  alleged  licensing 
violation and any  injury or damage to the claimant  that resulted from the 
routine rear -end collision.   We agree and reverse.  
 Limousines hired Catherine Rodriguez as a passenger shuttle bus  
driver .  Although Rodriguez held a valid Class B commercial driver’s  license, 
at issue is whether she had a valid passenger endorsement .  While driving 
an empty shuttle bus  several months later , Rodriguez failed to timely brake 
and made slight contact with the rear of Levit’s vehicle .  No injuries were 
reported at the scene.   
 3  Levit , together with the three passengers who occupied his vehicle at 
the time of the accident, filed a 32 -count  complaint , alleging various forms of 
negligence.  They subsequently  moved for leave to amend their complaint to 
seek punitive damages .  Levit filed a proffer arguing that Limousines’ 
decision to hire and permit Rodriguez to drive without the required passenger 
endorsement created an imminent danger and constituted intentional 
misconduct or gross negligence .  Following a hearing, t he trial court granted 
Levit’s motion, finding that permitting Rodriguez to transport passengers 
without the required endorsement  exposed the public to risk  and 
demonstrated a conscious disregard for the safety of others  sufficient to 
support punitive damages .1  
II. 
We review an order granting a motion for leave to amend to assert 
punitive damages de novo.  See McLane Foodservice Inc. v. Wool , 400 So. 
3d 757, 761 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024) (“Our de novo review similarly tests the 
sufficiency of the proffer in the light most favorable to the moving party, 
without accepting conclusory legal conclusions or labels such as ‘gross 
misconduct’ at face value. ” (citation omitted)).  
 
1 The trial court found that Levit met the statutory threshold to plead punitive 
damages based on intentional misconduct “and/or” gross negligence.   
 4 Section 768.72 , Florida Statutes , requires a “ reasonable showing by 
evidence in the record or proffered by the claimant ” that “ the defendant was 
personally guilty of intentional misconduct or gross negligence .”  § 
768.72 (1)–(2), Fla. Stat.  In Perlmutter v. Fed. Ins. Co. , the Florida Supreme 
Court recently held that the “clear and convincing” standard does not apply 
when the trial court evaluates the sufficiency of the claimant’s  evidentiary 
showing at the pleading stage.  434 So. 3d 681, 688 (Fla. 2026) .  It further 
confirmed “the test for deciding evidentiary sufficiency under section 
768.72(1) is whether a reasonable person could conclude, based on the claimant ’s evidence, that the defendant committed ‘intentional misconduct’ 
or ‘gross negligence,’ as defined in section 768.72(2).” Id.  (quoting § 
768.72 (1)–(2), Fla. Stat.).  
Punitive damages are available to address “egregious wrongdoing” 
that “constitutes a public wrong” and are imposed not to compensate the 
plaintiff, but for punishment and deterrence.  Id.  at 684 (citation omitted); see 
Manheimer v. Florida Power & Light Co. , 403 So. 3d 257 , 260  (Fla. 3d DCA 
2023)  (“[P]unitive  damages are reserved for truly culpable behavior and are 
intended to ‘express society ’s collective outrage. ’” (quoting KIS Grp., LLC v. 
Moquin , 263 So. 3d 63 , 65-66  (Fla. 4th DCA 2019) )). 
 
 5 A. 
“Intentional misconduct ” in the punitive damages context  means “ that 
the defendant had actual knowledge of the wrongfulness of the conduct and 
the high probability that injury or damage to the claimant would result and, 
despite that knowledge, intentionally pursued that course of conduct, 
resulting in injury or damage .” § 768.72 (2)(a), Fla. Stat.   The statute requires 
more than a knowing act —the  evide nce must demonstrate a defendant’s 
specific intent to pursue wrongful conduct despite actual knowledge of the 
high probability that injury would result. See Vaziri v. Jerkins , 400 So. 3d 634, 
638 (Fla. 4th DCA 2025)  (“proving intentional misconduct under section 
768.72(2)(a) requires evidence of ‘specific intent , not general intent, to 
knowingly engage in wrongful conduct .’” (quoting Fed. Ins. Co. v. Perlmutter , 
376 So. 3d 24 , 35 (Fla. 4th DCA 2023) , quashed  on other grounds , 434 So. 
3d 681, 688 (Fla. 2026)  (holding that the clear and convincing  standard does 
not govern the trial court’s evaluation of evidentiary  sufficiency at the 
pleading stage))) .  
A violation of a licensing or traffic statue, standing alone , does not 
satisfy that standard .  In Robertson v. Antoine , a forklift driver was driving on 
the wrong side of the roadway in violation of several statutes when he collided with a motorist —an act the trial court found sufficient to constitute 
 6 intentional misconduct . 423 So. 3d 910 , 911–16  (Fla. 4th DCA 2025) .  The 
Fourth District reversed, holding that although  the driver knowingly traveled 
against traffic, his mistaken belief that doing so was “safer” failed to 
demonstrate  “actual knowledge ” that his conduct was wrongful and there 
was “high probability”  injury would result —the conduct was “more properly 
characterized as ordinary negligence” and did not reflect the specific  intent  
required by the statue. Id. (quoting § 768.72 (2)(a) , Fla. Stat.).  The court 
specifically noted that “a party’s  violation of traffic law is, standing alone, an 
insufficient basis for punitive damages  . . .  there must be some additional 
act that shows the  [conduct] was reckless or a conscious disregard of or 
indifference to others” and found that no such “additional act” transformed  
the driver’s  decision to travel  against the flow of traffic into conduct sufficient 
to support punitive damages . Id. at 915 n.4 (citation omitted).  
Levit’s proffer fails at the threshold because it does not identify the 
intentional course of conduct required by section  768.72(2)(a).  A ny missing 
passenger endorsement is a licensing deficiency , not a course of conduct.  
The conduct resulting in Levit’s injury was Rodriguez’s operation of the 
shuttle —specifically her failure to timely brake —and the proffer contains no 
evidence that Rodriguez  intentionally drove in a wrongful manner despite 
actual knowledge that injury was highly probable.  As in Robertson , the 
 7 existence of a statutory or licensing violation, even if knowingly disregarded, 
does not supply the additional conduct necessary to transform ordinary 
negligence into intentional misconduct. 423 So. 3d at 911 –16.  Levit thus 
failed to proffer any conduct by Rodriguez or Limousines constituting the 
intentional course of conduct required by section 768.72 (2)(a).  
The licensing deficiency also bears no direct relation to the conduct 
that caused Levit’s  alleged  injury.  A punitive damages claim requires a direct 
link between the defendant’s conduct offered to support punitive damages and the plaintiff’s resulting harm. See Hardin v. R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. , 
314 So. 3d 584, 589 –91 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)  (holding that a punitive damages 
claim fails where there is no “direct link between the intentional wrongdoing by the defendant and the specific injuries to the plaintiff”).  Here, it is 
undisputed that there were no passengers in Rodriguez’s shuttle, Rodriguez 
held a valid commercial driver’s license and nothing in the proffer suggested that any endorsement deficiency impaired her ability to perceive traffic, brake 
or otherwise operate the vehicle.  Rather, t he accident was a minor rear -end 
collision caused by Rodriguez’s failure to brake on time.  The alleged 
endorsement deficiency thus bore no relation  to the conduct causing Levit’s 
alleged harm and, absent some additional act connecting that deficiency to 
knowing wrongdoing, cannot  transform an otherwise ordinary negligence 
 8 claim into one for intentional misconduc t. See State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. 
v. Campbell , 538 U.S. 408, 422 –23 (2003)  (finding the trial court erred when 
it “awarded punitive damages to punish and deter conduct that bore no 
relation to the [plaintiffs’]  harm ” and that the “ defendant ’s dissimilar acts, 
independent from the acts upon which liability was premised, may not serve 
as the basis for punitive damages ”).  
B. 
“Gross negligence”  for purposes of punitive damages  means  “that the 
defendant ’s conduct was so reckless or wanting in care that it constituted a 
conscious disregard or indifference to the life, safety, or rights of persons 
exposed to such conduct. ” § 768.72 (2)(b) , Fla. Stat.   The Florida Supreme 
Court has held that punitive damages “cannot be assessed for mere 
negligent conduct but  must be based on behavior which indicates a w anton 
disregard for the rights of others ” and that  “the required level of negligence 
for punitive damages is equivalent to the conduct involved in criminal 
manslaughter.” Valladares v. Bank of Am. Corp. , 197 So. 3d 1, 11 (Fla. 2016)  
(citation  omitted) . 
As with intentional  misconduct, a licensing or traffic violation  does not , 
standing alone, meet the heightened  gross negligence standard.  In Mercer 
v. Saddle Creek Transp., Inc. , the Sixth District  held that even though a 
 9 commercial truck driver appeared to violate a federal regulation prohibiting 
handheld cell phone use, “the mere use of a cell phone while driving a truck” 
does not “automatically provide[] a reasonable basis for a plaintiff to seek 
punitive damages.   There must be some additional act that shows the cell 
phone usage was reckless or a conscious disregard of or indifference to 
others to show gross negligence under  section 768.72(2)(b). ” 389 So. 3d 
774, 777 –78 (Fla. 6th DCA 2024) ; see Creech v. Santomassino , 395 So. 3d 
549, 553 –54 (Fla. 4th DCA 2024)  (holding that a driver’s “brief glance at his 
cell phone” without an y “additional act that shows the cell phone usage was 
reckless or a conscious disregard of or indifference to others ,” did not meet 
the gross negligence standard and  amounted to ordinary negligence at 
most ). 
In Mirlalda v. Mitchell, a commercial driver was alleged to be grossly 
negligent in failing to secure a pipe to his concrete -pump trailer because he 
had “an expired license when the accident occurred ,” “a history of driver’s  
license suspensions ” and “a similar accident two days earlier. ” 429 So. 3d 
1113, 11 16 (Fla. 6th DCA 2026) .   The Sixth District nevertheless concluded 
that those circumstances, considered “individually or collectively” failed to 
show that the driver’s conduct “was so reckless or wanting in care that it 
constituted a conscious disregard or indifference to the life or safety of the 
 10 people exposed to such conduct. ” Id. at 1120.  Individually, the court held 
that the above evidence was  irrelevant to gross negligence —although 
operating a vehicle with an expired license “was unlawful,” and a statutory 
traffic infraction , “the expiration of his license  alone is not evidence of his 
inability to operate” the vehicle and “malfeasance alone, ” “unrelated ” to 
harmful conduct  “does not support a finding of gross negligence. ” Id. at 1119.   
The court held that any  history of suspensions was not probative because 
they were not issued for “moving violations or reckless driving” but for 
administrative issues, and that the alleged prior accident was similarly 
irrelevant “without more” demonstrating that he “acted in a grossly negligent way.” Id. at 1119 –20.   
These cases make clear that a statutory or licensing violation, standing 
alone, does not support  punitive damages —the proffer must contain some  
“additional act” demonstrating  reckless ness  or a conscious disregard for the 
safety of others.  See id.; Mercer , 389 So. 3d at  777–78; Robertson , 423 So. 
3d at 911 -15.   
The trial court relied on Rodriguez’s and Limousine’s alleged 
knowledge of the licensing deficiency, reasoning that they nevertheless 
“allowed or permitted this conduct, thereby exposing passengers and the public to risk.”  But the trial court’s reasoning conflates the alleged existence 
 11 of a licensing deficiency with the conduct required by section 768.72(2)(b).  
Any missing passenger endorsement is a licensing deficiency, not conduct 
that was “so reckless or wanting in care” as to constitute a “conscious 
disregard or indifference to” the life, safety or rights of others. § 768.72(2)(b) , 
Fla. Stat.   Rather, the relevant conduct was Rodriguez ’s operation of the 
shuttle, and the proffer must demonstrate that her operation of the vehicle rose to that heightened level of culpability.  It did not.  
More specifically, the trial court reasoned that Limousines permitted 
Rodriguez  to drive  despite the alleged licensing deficiency and that doing so  
“in the course of transporting members of the public,  constitutes a 
reasonable evidentiary  basis for a finding of conscious disregard for the 
safety of others.”  But the premise underlying the trial court’s conclusion is  
simply unsupported by the proffer .  Levit ’s proffer specifically did not include 
any showing whatsoever that Rodriguez was carrying passengers at the time of the accident . A punitive damage determination cannot rest on a 
hypothetical worst -case scenario rather than the conduct that actually 
caused the harm. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 538 U.S. at 4 23 (“ Due 
process does not permit courts, in the calculation of punitive damages, to 
adjudicate the merits of other parties ’ hypothetical claims against a 
defendant under the guise of the reprehensibility analysis [.]”). 
 12 The accident was a routine rear -end collision apparently caused by 
Rodriguez’s failure to timely brake .  These circumstances would not lead a 
“reasonable person to conclude” that Rodriguez or Limousines  engaged in 
conduct  “so reckless or wanting in care that it constituted a conscious 
disregard or indifference to the life, safety, or rights of persons exposed to 
such conduct .” § 768.72(2)(b), Fla. Stat.; s ee Perlmutter , 434 So. 3d at  688 
(Fla. 2026) .  At most, any conduct  amount ed to ordinary negligence and fell 
well short of the manslaughter equivalent standard required for punitive 
damages. See Valladares , 197 So. 3d at 11.   
We find the alleged licensing deficiency also lacks the requisite nexus 
to Levit’s gross negligence claim.  Any missing passenger endorsement bore 
no direct relation to Rodriguez’s failure to timely brake or the resulting 
collision. See Ebsary Found. Co. v. Servinsky , 378 So. 3d 625 , 626  (Fla. 4th 
DCA 2023)  (finding that a proffer is insufficient when the “ proffered evidence 
is not directly related ” to the alleged gross negligence).  Nor did Levit proffer 
any additional conduct connecting the licensing deficiency to the heightened  
culpability required for gross negligence .  See Mirlalda , 429 So. 3d at 1119 –
20.   
In sum, Levit failed to proffer evidence demonstrating the specific intent 
required for intentional misconduct or the conscious disregard necessary for 
 13 gross negligence.  It is paramount that trial courts understand their proper 
gatekeeping role when reviewing proffers to determine whether they meet 
the statutory requirements for punitive  damages. “Becau se punitive 
damages are meant to be reserved for the most egregious of cases and have 
substantial impacts to the parties, section 768.72  requires the trial court to 
act as a gatekeeper and preclude a claim for punitive damages where there is no reasonable evidentiary basis for recovery.”  See Manheimer , 403 So. 
3d at 261 (citation modified) .  It is well recognized that “t he granting of a 
motion for leave to amend a complaint to add a punitive damages claim can 
be a ‘game changer ’ in litigation. ” TRG Desert Inn Venture, Ltd. v. 
Berezovsky, 194 So. 3d 516, 520  n.5 (Fla. 3d DCA 2016).  “Allowing a 
plaintiff to proceed with a punitive damages claim subjects the defendant to 
financial discovery that would otherwise be off limits, and potentially subjects 
the defendant to uninsured losses .” Id. (citation omitted).  For that reason, 
punitive damages “are reserved for truly culpable conduct  . . . so outrageous 
in character, and so extreme in degree that the facts of the case to an average member of the community would arouse his resentment against the 
actor, and lead him to exclaim, ‘Outrageous!’ ” McLane Foodservice Inc. , 400 
So. 3d at 762 (citation omitted).  No such facts exist here.   
 14 Reversed  and remanded for further proceedings consistent with this 
opinion.

items.summary:
In a substituted opinion, the Third DCA reversed leave to plead punitive damages arising from a rear-end collision. An alleged missing passenger endorsement, without additional culpable conduct or a direct connection to the claimant’s harm, did not establish intentional misconduct or gross negligence. Applying Perlmutter, the court explained that the pleading-stage question is whether a reasonable person could find the statutory misconduct from the proffer; clear and convincing proof is not required at that stage. Rehearing and certification were denied, and the earlier opinion was withdrawn.

Holding: A licensing violation alone, without additional culpable conduct and a nexus to the alleged harm, did not provide a reasonable evidentiary basis for punitive damages on this record.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded; earlier opinion withdrawn and substituted; rehearing and certification denied.

The Third DCA affirmed by citation to authorities on construing an insurance policy together with its application, endorsements and riders; selecting nonstacking uninsured-motorist coverage; and the signed-form presumption under section 627.727(1) (2017). The opinion gives no independent factual account. Policy language and facts quoted from the cited cases should not be treated as findings about Dorticos's policy.

Holding: The court affirmed by citation to whole-policy construction principles, authorities addressing informed election of nonstacking uninsured-motorist coverage, and the signed-form presumption in section 627.727(1) (2017). This citation opinion supplies those grounds but no case-specific factual explanation; facts quoted from cited cases must not be attributed to Dorticos.

items.summary:
The Third DCA affirmed with citations concerning foreclosure standing and summary judgment. The cited authorities require the nonmovant to identify a genuine, material factual dispute and explain proof of standing through an endorsed note, including adequately explained differences between an original and its copy. The opinion also cites authority supporting proof of an acceleration notice through an affidavit, the letter, and mailing records. It provides no detailed factual narrative, so these cited principles should not be presented as findings about particular documents in this case.

Holding: Citation affirmance applying summary-judgment, note-holder standing, and acceleration-notice authorities.

Disposition: Affirmed.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  October 21, 2026 . 
 
________________  
 
No. 3D26-0622  
Lower Tribunal No. 21-5636 -GD-02 
________________  
 
 
Arys Rene Cabrera , 
Petitioner , 
 
vs. 
 
Lilian Guadalupe Cabrera Rubio, etc., et al. , 
Respondents . 
 
 
 
 On Petiti on for Writ of Certiorari from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County , Jorge E. Cueto , Judge.  
 
 Kenneth M. Kaplan,  for petitioner . 
 
 Get Ahead Legal, and Irama Valdes;  Soren & Gallardo, P.A. , and 
Christin Gallardo  and Max G. Soren , for respondent  Lilian Guadalupe 
Cabrera Rubio . 
 
  
Before  SCALES , C.J., and  MILL ER and GOOD EN, JJ.  
 
PER CURIAM.  
 
 2   Petitioner Arys Rene Cabrera challenges, via certiorari, the 
guardianship court’s February 26, 2026 omnibus order rendered after a 
hearing  of the same day  (the “Order”). The Order, among other things, 
denied Petitioner’s motion to remove Respondent  Lilian Guadalupe Cabrera 
Rubio  as the guardian for the ward. Petitioner asserts standing as an 
“interested person” under section 744.477(1) of the Florida Statutes  (2025) .1  
The Order adjudicates with finality  Petitioner’s right  as an interested 
person to seek the removal of the guardian. See Fla. R. App. P. 9.170(b)  
(“[A]ppeals of orders rendered in . . . guardianship cases  will be limited to 
orders that finally determine a right or obligation of an interested person as 
defined in the Florida Probate Code.”); see Hernandez v. Hernandez , 230 
So. 3d 119, 123 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017). Because section 744.477(1) provided 
Petitioner with the right to seek the guardian’s removal, the trial court’s denial 
of the Petition to Remove Guardian “on the merits” constituted a final order.  
We therefore treat the petition as an appeal of the Order . See Fla. R. 
App. P.  9.040(c)  (“If a party seeks an improper remedy, the cause must be 
treated as if the proper remedy had been sought[.]”) .2 We have carefully 
 
1 Under the Florida Probate Code, an interested person is “any person who 
may reasonably be expected to be affected by the outcome of the particular 
proceeding involved.” § 731.201(23), Fla. Stat. (2026).  
 
 3 reviewed the parties’ extensive briefing, the Order, and those portions of the 
record provided to us by the parties, including the statement of proceedings 
that Petitioner filed pursuant to Florida Rule of Appellate  Procedure  
9.200(b)(5) , in lieu of a transcript of the February 26, 2026  hearing.  Earlier in 
this appeal, w e also considered and ruled on certain  procedural issues 
related to Petitioner’s action , and thus we are informed  by the  facts and 
issues  we necessarily considered in that prior adjudication . Cabrera v. 
Rubio , 51 Fla. L. Weekly D782, 2026 WL 1014066  (Fla. 3d DCA Apr. 15, 
2026).   
Because Petitioner has established no basis for reversal of the Order , 
we affirm the Order in all respects.  Also, because g uardianship resources 
are limited and should be used for the benefit of the ward, no motion for 
rehearing or any other post -opinion motion will be entertained by the Court.   
Petition for writ of certiorari treated as appeal ; challenged Order 
affirmed.  
 
 
2 We note that, had we reviewed the Order under the certiorari standard, we 
would have been compelled to dismiss the petition for lack of jurisdiction 
because Petitioner failed to establish that he, as opposed to the ward, had 
suffered irreparable harm. See Aguilar v. Leal , 426 So. 3d 1277, 1278 (Fla. 
3d DCA 2026).

items.summary:
The Third DCA treated a certiorari petition as an appeal because denial on the merits of an interested person's statutory guardian-removal request finally determined that right under rule 9.170(b). It affirmed without developing the underlying removal merits. The court alternatively explained that certiorari would require irreparable harm to the petitioner, not merely the ward. Its direction barring rehearing and other post-opinion motions applies to this case, not appeals generally.

Holding: A merits order denying an interested person’s statutory request to remove a guardian finally determines that right and is appealable under rule9.170(b); the court treated the certiorari petition as an appeal under rule9.040(c). The opinion alternatively explains that certiorari would require irreparable harm to the petitioner, not merely to the ward.

Disposition: Petition for writ of certiorari treated as appeal; challenged order affirmed in all respects. No rehearing or other post-opinion motion will be entertained in this case.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  October 21, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D26 -0182  
Lower Tribunal No. 25-191003 -CC-23 
________________  
 
 
Boris Jean -Philippe Vulac , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
CVAR International LLC , 
Appellee.  
 
 
 An Appeal from the County  Court for Miami -Dade County, Natalie 
Moore , Judge.  
 
 Boris Jean -Philippe Vulac , in proper person . 
 
 Kelley & Grant, P.A. , and Cory S. Carano (Boca Raton) , for appellee.  
 
 
Before  FERNANDEZ, LOGUE, and BOKOR , JJ.  
 
 PER CURIAM.  
 In his challenge to his landlord’s eviction action, the Appellant -Tenant 
waived his defense of lack of personal jurisdiction due to improper service 
 2 by filing a permissive counterclaim seeking $50,000 for emotional distress 
and reputational damage. Celebrity Actors Camp, Inc. v. Bredbenner , 394 
So. 3d 782, 786 (Fla. 2d DCA 2024) (holding parties that filed an answer and 
a counterclaim seeking affirmative relief submitted themselves to jurisdiction 
of the court regardless of defective service).  
He was therefore required to pay  into the registry of the court the 
accrued rent because he was interposing defenses not based on his 
payment of the rent.  See § 83.60(2) , Fla. Stat.  (“In an action by the landlord 
for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other 
than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3 -day 
notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accr ued rent as 
alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that 
accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due. The clerk shall 
notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons. Failure of the tenant 
to pay the rent into t he registry of the court or to file a motion to determine 
the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding 
Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process 
constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant ’s defenses other than payment, 
and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of 
 3 the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing 
thereon.”) .  
Once it was established that Appellant failed to pay the rent into the 
court registry, the trial court was constrained to enter a default judgment of 
removal of the tenant with a writ of possession.  1560 -1568 Drexel Ave., LLC 
v. Dalton , 320 So. 3d 965, 969 (Fla. 3d DCA 2021) (“Section 83.60(2) is not 
discretionary; it compels a tenant defending against an eviction to pay into 
the court registry either (i) the amount of rent alleged to be due, or (ii) the 
amount of rent determined by the  court, plus all rent that accrues during the 
case ’s pendency.”).  
Affirmed.

items.summary:
The Third DCA held that a tenant waived an improper-service personal-jurisdiction defense by filing a permissive counterclaim seeking affirmative relief. It also affirmed the removal judgment and writ of possession for failure to comply with the residential rent-registry requirement. The quoted statute allows a timely motion to determine the rent amount and excludes weekends and legal holidays from its five-day period. This dwelling-unit rule is not presented as a categorical rule for commercial leases.

Holding: A tenant waived an improper-service personal-jurisdiction defense by filing a permissive counterclaim seeking affirmative relief. With defenses other than payment, section 83.60(2) required compliance with the residential rent-registry procedure; on this record, failure to pay into the registry required a default judgment removing the tenant and a writ of possession. The statute quoted by the court also allows a timely motion to determine the rent amount.

Disposition: Affirmed.

Author: Per curiam

DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA  
FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
BROWARD CARE AT HOME, LLC, 
ATLANTIC HOME HEALTH AGENCY OF SOUTH FLORIDA, LLC, 
HOMECARE PARTNERS MANAGEMENT, LLC, 
DAVID CHRIS RUCKER, RYAN RUSKIN,  
BRIAN JOHNSON, and JAMES SPRIGS, 
Appellants, 
 
v. 
 
ANDREW SHOOK and ASSIST NURSING AGENCY, LLC, 
Appellees. 
 
No. 4D2026-0220 
 
[October 21, 2026] 
 
Appeal of a nonfinal order from the Circuit Court for the Seventeenth 
Judicial Circuit, Broward County; Carlos A. Rodriguez, Judge; L.T. Case 
No. 062024CA005197AXXXCE.  
 
Samuel B. Spinner of Carlton Fields, Miami, and David J. Carrier of 
Carlton Fields, Minneapolis, Minnesota, Pro Hac Vice, for appellants. 
 
Brigid F. Cech Samole and Elizabeth C. Sardinas of Greenberg Traurig, 
P.A., Miami, for appellees. 
 
PER CURIAM . 
 
We reverse the order granting the plaintiff leave to amend his complaint 
to assert punitive damages claims.  Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.190 
requires the proposed amended pleading to be attached to the motion and 
served at least twenty days before the hearing.  Cowan v. Levai , 427 So. 
3d 147, 150–51 (Fla. 3d DCA 2025); Taylor v. City of Lake Worth, 964 So. 2d 243, 244 (Fla. 4th DCA 2007).  The plaintiff neither attached the 
proposed amended complaint to his motion nor filed his proposed amended complaint until seven days before the hearing. 
 Reversed and remanded. 
 M
AY, GROSS and S HEPHERD , JJ., concur.  
 
2 
 *            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
The Fourth DCA reversed an order granting leave to add punitive-damages claims because the plaintiff did not attach the proposed amended complaint to the motion and filed it only seven days before the hearing. The court stated that rule 1.190 requires the proposed pleading to accompany the motion and be served at least twenty days before the hearing.

Holding: Leave to plead punitive damages was improperly granted without the proposed amended pleading attached to the motion and served at least twenty days before the hearing.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded.
